video_description: Yesterday, I gave my inaugural speech to parliament. As per tradition, I took the chance to thank my friends, family and loved ones (including my now-fiancée, Noah!). But I also highlighted some of the issues people have raised across Preston and Reservoir, and some of the policies we’re prioritising.
transcript:

I'd like to begin by acknowledging the Wurundjeri people, upon whose land we are gathered, and
I'd like to begin by thanking the people of Preston and Reservoir for electing me
as their representative.
Elections are this wonderful opportunity for all of us to have this great big collective
discussion about government, and we knocked on about 5,000 doors and we were lucky to
have a remarkably diverse set of conversations about all of the ways in which the words
and actions of government touch upon the lives of the people of Preston and Reservoir.
I'd like to give a shout out to Steve and Laura in West Preston who talked to us
about climate change. I'd like to shout out to Amalia also in West Preston who
really, really liked the idea of bringing back the SEC.
A shout out to Nicole in Keon Park who talked to us about the chAllanges of crossing the
railway line. For reasons that I don't fully understand, when they built the
railway line in Reservoir, they built about a two kilometre stretch that has no
rail crossings. I don't know if any other members have a stretch that long in an
established suburb with no crossing, but it's certainly a long way for those
who perhaps live on one side and have their child zoned into a school on the other.
You have to go all the way down and back again. It's known sometimes locally as
the Berlin Wall for that reason. For a long time, historically, the problem
was those crossings, as a result, were very congested. Anyway, I'm very proud
to be part of a Labor government, and indeed the first government in a
hundred years to do something about that problem, which is that we have
made it easier to cross at Reservoir Station, fixing one of the worst

video_description: Today, I spoke in parliament to ask the Minister for Planning to protect the Preston Market.
transcript:
My adjournment matter is for the Minister for Planning, and the action I seek is that
the Minister protects the Preston Market. I know the Minister has been reading through
a great deal of material about the market, and I know she is a very regular visitor.
She is often up our way, and I would like to take this opportunity to thank her for
the diligent and thoughtful way in which she has approached this important issue
for our community. I understand that the Minister is now
in a position where she is close to being able to make some decisions about the market,
and in that respect, I specifically ask that she protects the centreway and its surrounding
buildings and keeps them in their current location.
We have knocked on hundreds of doors around the market, and that is what has clearly
emerged from our community. What people want to be able to do is to walk down
the centreway or walk through the deli or maybe the seafood section, and they want
to be able to experience the great, vibrant, multicultural, affordable market that they
can experience today. I know that is important to me, and I know it is also important to
the member for Northcote and the member for Pascoe Vale, good Labor members who
know their multicultural communities very well, and of course know the market well
through their own Greek and Italian families. Speaker, that is not the same, I should
be clear, as saying that nothing can ever change at the market. We are not asking
the Minister to build a new sovereign hill of sorts where everything is just frozen
in place for all time. There is a strong case for making the market
more environmentally sensitive. There is a strong case for improving some aspects
of its operations, its sewerage system and some of the other essential services
upon which the traders rely. There is a case, Speaker, for making a better use
of the whole site. The Save the Preston Market Group have put forward a proposal
where some of the current car parks are used for mid-rise buildings, and if that
were done thoughtfully and incrementally, we could imagine that making the market
an even better place. But most fundamentally, Speaker, I am rising today
to ask that any such upgrades keep the heart of the market as it currently is,
so as people go there and they get their fresh pasta, their Asian groceries,
whatever they might get on a Saturday morning, we would like to make sure that
any upgrades enhance or support that part of the market rather than displacing
or destroying it. I thank the Minister for her consideration of this important
issue for our community.

video_description:
A message from the Premier for Keon Park! 

-- with @[134712696593275:274:Dan Andrews] and @[100058217675236:2048:Bronwyn Halfpenny MP]
transcript:
It's great to be in Keon Park here today to mark significant milestones in the removal
of this dangerous and congested level crossing, as well as a brand new station. There's 18,000
vehicles pass through this busy level crossing every day and the boon gates are down for
more than 40 minutes of every peak. It's dangerous, it's congested, it's got to
go, we're getting on and doing exactly what we said we'd do. Early works are
well under way, undergrounding all these power lines and moving a whole lot of
other services. And it's great to be able to meet with the workers here today who are
doing a fantastic job. We're on track and this community simply won't recognise how
good it's going to be. No more level crossing, being able to get where you need to go safer
and sooner, and it's Labor delivering what matters and doing all the things we
said we would do. Now I'm joined by two local champions, people who stand up for
their local community and do a great job. Bronwyn, over to you.
Thank you Premier. Look, locals, we're all really excited about the removal of this
level crossing. The amount of time you spend in traffic, the Premier's already
talked about, but also we're really excited about the public space that's
going to open up underneath the bridge. There's going to be hopefully, you know,
bike paths and places where people can park, recreation areas, and there's not much
around this area that's here, so it's going to make the area look fantastic.
I think everybody's going to be excited, and we're all looking forward to it.
The finest course the road works.
Thank you.
I just agree with Bronwyn. We've talked to a lot of households, a lot of businesses in the area.
Certainly people are excited about being easy to drive around, but I think exactly
as you say, the fact that it'll be easier to walk around and cycle around,
and particularly really grateful to the project team for doing some great work
in response to some feedback from the community, and now opening it up so you're
going to walk from Johnson Street basically along in a line across the Hughes
Parade to really help open up this area. It'll be good for the businesses on
Johnson Street, it'll be good for the whole feel of the area, and it'll integrate
with the open space that Bronwyn was talking about, and of course,
ultimately, also make our public transport system better when we get more trains
more often, and it'll be easy to get to the station because of all the
improvements that we've put in place.
That's the whole thing. It's about jobs, it's about more trains more often,
it's about a road network that actually works, it's about safety, and
ultimately, it's about making sure the communities are essentially united
and have got extra public space and the sort of amenity that everyone is
entitled to, a station that everybody can access.
You've got to get things done, and this is a great example of pushing
on and doing what matters. We are delighted, and I'll be pleased to be
back again to mark other milestones on this really significant project.
The last word, of course, has to be thank you to all the apprentices,
trainees, cadets, the engineers, all the workers who are doing an amazing
job at this level crossing. We've got 68 of these gone, and 110 of them
will be gone by 2030. That's Labor doing what matters.

video_description: Last week, I asked the Minister for Roads and Road Safety, @[100058234262537:2048:Melissa Horne MP], for an update regarding the Boldrewood and Broadway roundabout.
transcript:
My question is also for the Minister for Roads and Road Safety, and I ask what consideration
has her department given to modifying or improving the roundabout at Baldrude Parade
and Broadway in Reservoir East. I draw her attention quickly to three chAllanges with
this busy intersection. First, it has five roads going into it, including Strathmerton
Street, which intersects at a very close angle to Baldrude Parade, making it hard
for users to judge where vehicles are exiting. It is, secondly, a two-lane roundabout,
which is a generally unfriendly format for pedestrians and cyclists, and it is situated
close to a number of community facilities that people walk and ride to, including a
primary school. Thirdly, it has above average speeds due to its slope, its generous cornering
and its current 60 km per hour limit. Those things in combination would raise
the eyebrows of traffic engineers and road safety experts generally. They are a source
of concern for nearby residents and all of us that use the intersection, and
I thank the Minister for her consideration.

Today, we tabled the @[100071960739450:2048:Save the Preston Market] petition. Some of the signatures were from last year, and some things have changed since then, but the general message of the petition hasn't.

(Also thanks to Jake who was doing work experience for helping count them all, if that's not a classic work experience task I don't know what is 😊)
transcript:

Order. Order. The question is that these petitions be tabled. Member for Preston.

video_description:
Over the last two weeks, I’ve received hundreds of emails and messages about the events in Israel, Gaza and the West Bank. 

We have all been horrified by the suffering and loss.

Many government MPs spoke about the issue in parliament this week. Our contributions reflected our different perspectives, but we were united in our belief that the priority for the Victorian Government must be our own multicultural communities.

Thousands of Palestinian and Jewish Victorians have friends or family caught up in the conflict. Many are fearful and anxious. Social media content can compound their anxiety. One-sided posts that fail to acknowledge Palestinian suffering circulate in our Muslim communities, and one-sided posts that fail to acknowledge Israeli suffering circulate in our Jewish communities.

The priority for the Victorian Labor Government, as the Premier has made clear, is to provide love and support to all Victorians who have friends or family in Israel, Gaza or the West Bank, regardless of their religion or race. The last two weeks have been incredibly tragic for some, and traumatic for most. People who have spent their lives hoping for peace have seen it ripped away again.

We have spoken with affected local residents. Our thoughts are with them. We will provide any support we can during this time of worry, suffering and grief.
transcript:
Deputy Speaker, some members of our family live on a mashev near the Gaza Strip. They
are okay in the sense that they have not been physically harmed by the recent attacks,
but their lives will never be the same again. War is always full of horrors, but people
going from door to door, murdering and terrorising non-combatants in front of their families
is a special kind of horror. It wasn't Maile, it wasn't Deir Yassin and it
wasn't Eshkol. Thousands of innocent Palestinian men, women and children have also been
killed, including the family members of our fellow Victorians. Our hearts go out to them.
When their family has been killed by Israeli bombs, they will be rightfully devastated
and angry. I have spoken with APAN, I have spoken
with local Palestinians, I have spent time in Ramallah. I think we all agree that
as this conflict continues, we should try to be as humane as possible in our comments,
acknowledge the suffering on both sides and distinguish between the actions of
people and the actions of their leaders. And Speaker, we must keep in mind that
our responsibilities as Victorian MPs in a sub-national government are to our own
multicultural and multi-faith communities. I don't think Deputy Speaker
that any of us should be out trying to win votes by making divisive
comments about a tragic overseas conflict. We hope for peace and our
thoughts are with everyone whose families are suffering and grieving.

Thanks to Michael Longmore from Merri Creek Management Committee and Nick Williams from @[100064273856632:2048:Friends of Merri Creek] for talking to us about their exciting new Green Links project. 🌿
transcript:
So we're down here on the banks of the Merri Creek with the fantastic team from the Merri
Creek Management Committee and we've just had the very exciting news this week that
there will be a significant amount of funding provided to the committee through our Green
Links Fund to do some very important revegetation work and re-wilding work here along the
creek. And I'm hoping, maybe Michael, you can just explain what it is that you
plan to do with the funds that we've announced this week.
Yeah, so we're hoping that over the next three years we'll plant around 17,000 trees
and shrubs and grasses and all sorts of things to create a series of wildlife refuge
areas in Coburg, Thornbury, Northcote and Brunswick East. Those will help provide
shelter for wallabies and small birds, things that are currently getting skied off
by the public. And reintroduce the habitat that's missing from this part of the creek.

with nature in an area which becomes a lot more natural which will be a lot better for the biodiversity.

hoping to improve, what does it look like at the moment when we wander through?

the vegetated areas are mostly full of weeds. So we'll be working to get rid of
most of those weeds and replace them with native species which have better
benefits for biodiversity and provide habitat for various animals.
So by changing from weeds to native species it's a lot better for the food chain.
We've got all those native insects and the native birds will follow that.
It will also be great habitat for wallabies which need to sort of
refuge during the day in deep, deep vegetation. So that'll be really good for that
and people get to see that wildlife a little bit more often too.

but we need to protect them?

on one side of the creek and the other side of the creek for the wildlife corridor.

but also some fencing to keep dogs off leach out of those areas.

but these areas will be refuges where people can go and enjoy that nature
and the nature will have a bit of space for itself as well.

the Merri Creek Management website and on our social media pages.
So follow our social media and you'll find out about it.

Social media age limitations — have your say before Friday (survey link in comments)
transcript:
The Victorian Government is currently running a survey on age limitations for social media
and if you're at all interested I'd encourage you to fill it out.
It's important to be clear this is not about introducing fines or penalties for young people
for using their phones, there won't be any of that. Rather it is about introducing penalties
for the companies that make these applications and who allow young people to use them in ways
that we now know are harmful and the hope is that in the long run that will encourage them
to develop more age-appropriate versions of their technology. It is striking at the moment
in Australia that a 13-year-old can walk into an Apple Store for instance and purchase an iPhone
that can obviously access and do all of the things that an adult iPhone can do. That's not the case
in other countries and you can certainly imagine a world in which that 13-year-old
could still have a phone but there would be restrictions on the apps that could be downloaded
and there are restrictions on those apps themselves to ensure that the experience
was safer and more positive for that 13-year-old and the same goes for children
as they get older and older. So if you have any thoughts on what that might look like,
what the problems are, the possible solutions, how we get the balance right between the
positive and negative bits of social media, please fill out the survey. The deadline is
Friday, that's this Friday. The link will be in the comments or else you can just Google
Victorian Government Social Media Survey.

transcript:
Hi everyone, I just want to provide an update on the effects of new planning laws on the
Merrilands Restrictive Covenant. These laws technically haven't passed the Parliament
yet but they have been approved by Labor and Green MPs in the Upper House and I have
no doubt that they will pass in the new year. And in essence the changes give Darebin
Council or VCAT the discretion to remove the Covenant through the normal planning
permit process. And I think it is likely that either Council or VCAT will do that
for a significant number of subdivisions and multi dwelling developments in this area.
So it is a big change. Now the Covenant will continue to have an effect and probably
the best way to explain it is that if you go back five years it used to often be
the case that someone trying to subdivide in any general residential zone often faced
a long battle that ended up in VCAT but then they would win in VCAT anyway unless
they were doing something unusual. With our housing statement reforms we have dramatically
sped up that process for building new homes because you can no longer appeal a
development to VCAT unless it is doing something unusual. However all of those
old requirements around notice to neighbors, objections, Council
consideration, VCAT consideration all that will continue to apply for
properties covered by restrictive Covenants. So in effect it's become
easier to build housing in general residential zones but now restrictive
Covenant areas have become like the old general residential zones and I
suspect that will mean that larger developers don't look to Marylands
because they will want to go and build somewhere where their pathway to
development is faster. But for people who own land in Marylands and want to
subdivide it no doubt some of them will try to do that as soon as the
new laws come into effect in 2027 and I imagine they will have a
reasonable success rate in removing the Covenant particularly in those
areas marked in Darraben Council's housing strategy in orange that are
marked for increased change along High Street, Mahoneys Road, Radford Road
and the areas near the train station I think it's very likely that
applications to remove the Covenant to remove the Covenant will be successful
there. So none of this is legal advice and as many people know restrictive
Covenants are complex instruments and we're still trying to understand how
Council decisions and VCAT decisions will affect the Marylands one but I
just wanted to convey the general gist of the changes because I know the
Covenant is a significant topic of discussion in the community it's very
popular among a lot of people and I think it's just important to be really
clear that these changes will reduce the strength of the Covenant and lead
to more multi-dwelling development in this area in the long run.

BULLANTS UPDATE — we will speak to the AFL this week about the Bullants and the future of standalone VFLW/VFL clubs
transcript:
Hi everyone, this is an update on the Bullants VFL Club. As many of you will remember, the AFL
terminated the Bullants licence in October last year and the club entered voluntary liquidation
in December. This week we're meeting with the AFL to ask them two key questions about that.
First, why was the licence terminated so abruptly, particularly given that in previous
seasons, notably in 2023, there had been the opportunity for a broader discussion and
for governments at all levels to provide some support. And then secondly, and probably more
importantly looking forward, how is the AFL going to guarantee the survival of standalone clubs,
either VFL or VFLW, that don't have access to pokies revenue and aren't affiliated with an AFL
club and cross-subsidised by them. Now, there are of course some important differences between
the VFL and the VFLW in terms of how they operate, but that key question about standalone
clubs is the same. We have been lucky locally that Kat Theophanous MP, our fantastic Labor
Northcote MP has secured some funding recently for the Falcons. Ged Kearney has secured $700,000 for
change room upgrades and Mayor Emily Dimitriadis and Councillor Kristine Olaris, who was Mayor
last year, have secured some funding for lighting. So it's important to be clear that
overall the Falcons are in no way in the same position as the Bullants, but nonetheless,
it is still the AFL who make these key decisions about the future of VFLW clubs,
just as they do VFL clubs. And so we will take the opportunity to ask about both.
If you have any questions or issues related to that, that you think we should ask the AFL,
let us know. And then there is the second separate but related issue about the future
of Preston City Oval and its winter tenants. So over summer, the Preston Cricket Club have
been playing here. They'll continue to do so. They're going very well, but there have been
two suggestions made about winter. Firstly, there are of course two other Preston Bullants
clubs locally, the Juniors at Zwarr and the Amateurs at Ruthven. One option is for those
clubs to become winter tenants or at least play more games here and in that way preserve the
143 year legacy of the Bullants and potentially build the base for a VFL return. Alternatively,
there is the view that this is an elite level ground. It should host elite level sides. And
realistically, that's either the Northern Knights or Darabin Falcons VFLW or both.
Ultimately, that question is a question for Darabin Council. It's their asset.
It may be that if they're a bit more hands on in the way they manage it compared to
the past, they might be able to support both of those ideas to a degree. But if you have any
views on that, please contact your local councillor or send them to us and we can
send it to them. If you have any points for the AFL specifically, then let us know and we
can raise those with them this week.

Hi everyone, just an update on some industrial relations matters. Obviously the big news
this week was that government school staff stopped work on Tuesday with respect to the
VGSA agreement. The headline figures there are that the offer on the table is approximately
18 per cent over four years and the unions involved in the negotiations are seeking
approximately 35 per cent. The AEU, who are the main union on that agreement, are
also currently negotiating the Vectea and Triple EA agreements for early childhood professionals.
The headline offer there is 39.6 per cent over four years for educators and to match
school teacher pay sky levels for early childhood teachers. And then locally there
is also the possibility that Darebin Council staff and workers may take protected industrial
action soon. I believe they are seeking 22 per cent over four years. I'm not sure
if that had an offer back. People watching television may have also noticed ABC workers
are on strike at the moment or certainly were yesterday. But one important thing
to say about all of these public sector agreements is that while the headline figures
are crucial, there is a lot of detail in them. They normally run to over 100
and traditionally public sector agreements have been a chance to push forward some important
progressive reforms, things like reproductive leave, gender affirmation leave, work from home
arrangements, other flexible work arrangements. And of course, they've also been a chance to
deal with some of the inequality that deals, that appears within the pay scales of the
agreement. So often the average pay scale in a public sector agreement will be around
$120,000 a year, but there will be some people on easily more than double that,
some people on less than half that, and these discussions and negotiations are a chance to
reduce that gap. AU members in particular will be aware that the union settled the TAFE
agreement last year for I think 21 per cent over four years with some important
changes to workloads and that disparity of classifications, and we do hope to see
similar good outcomes with respect to this year's agreements. I won't try and run through
every other agreement that the Victorian Government is currently involved in because
there's always a lot, but I just want to recognise local UFU firefighters who make a
big contribution to our community, both professionally and personally, and who have
now been involved in unresolved negotiations regarding their agreements since July of 2020.
Obviously, if you're a union member, you should be well informed about where your own
agreements are up to, and of course you do have the right to take protected industrial
action as legalised by the Keating Labor Government and the right to negotiate across
multiple employers as Darrabin are doing as legalised by the Albanese Labor Government,
but we are very happy to answer any general questions people might have or to pass on
feedback to the relevant portfolios, ministers or public sector organisations involved in these discussions.

campaign to upgrade the lighting here has finally come together with the announcement
today of an additional $250,000 contribution from our Victorian Labor Government. And
as local residents will know, there are of course light towers here already, but
they're mainly old metal halide lights. They're very inefficient and they've been
too weak for clubs to train under. And in fact, the former Northern Bullants
VFL side, who of course were here, ended up spending tens of thousands of dollars
every season to hire grounds elsewhere so that they could train in the evenings.
And as history has shown, that was probably money they couldn't afford.
We do really wish in hindsight that the project could have come together a little
faster for them. But it is nonetheless great news for the Darebin Falcons VFL
side, who have been facing exactly the same issue, spending lots and lots of
money training at Latrobe and RMIT, Bundura and other grounds with decent
lighting. And it's also good news for the other two co-tenants here, the
Northern Knights and the Preston Cricket Club.
And while today's announcement is a state government announcement, a lot of
credit must go to Ged Kearney, our local Federal Labor MP.
It was Ged last year who secured seven hundred thousand dollars to upgrade
the change rooms here for female players and gender diverse players.
That is an upgrade that is very much needed.
And it was Ged's announcement that led to council bringing forward seven
hundred thousand dollars of their money for the lighting.
That led to the AFL providing another two hundred thousand dollar grant and now
to the state government providing our contribution.
And hopefully within that total budget, nearly two million dollars, the lights
and the change rooms can both be upgraded properly so that this fantastic
historic community facility can be a bit safer, more inclusive and better
utilised by the community.
And I know there are some discussions going on right at the moment on that
topic with Preston Bulance amateurs and juniors and other clubs about
increasing the local community use to make the most of this significant
investment. I do want to recognise quickly the contribution of Mayor
Emily Demetriades and local councillor Kristine Olaris in pulling
this project together. And then finally, on a different topic, we've also had
some good news from our meetings with the AFL and the Minister for Sport
regarding the systematic financial disadvantage faced by standalone VFL,
W and VFL clubs like the Bulance, like the Falcons.
There is widespread recognition that that is a problem, that something has
to be done about it. And we're hoping to see some further announcements
about it later this year.
Thanks for watching!

An update regarding the Pavilion school — if you have any questions, let us know

@[100058217675236:2048:Bronwyn Halfpenny MP] @[100057960313840:2048:Colin Brooks MP]
transcript:
We were here at the Fantastic Sylvester Hive Community Garden in East Preston a couple
of weekends ago and one of the issues that people raised was the ongoing rumour that
the Pavilion School, the school behind us here, was closing down and I just want to
say that rumour is completely untrue. The school is not closing down and in fact there
have been no changes at all to the state government support for Pavilion or for other
flexible learning campuses. What has changed is two things. Firstly, there has been
an increase in the rent that the Pavilion School pays at its Epping campus, at its
other campus, and second there have been some financial chAllanges at Charles La Trobe
College which is the biggest school that Pavilion is part of and there have been some
staffing cuts and some public debate within the school community about how that has
affected Pavilion compared to other campuses. Now in response to those issues a reference
group has been formed or is being formed which will bring together people from different
parts of the school, different parts of the school community and seek in the first instance
just to establish a bit more of a common understanding of the facts here with regard
to the resourcing chAllanges and the staffing changes and then once it's done that it
will look at the bigger question of what the best governance model is for the Pavilion
School in the long run. But just to be really clear again the school is not closing
down and in fact we all recognise the really important role that it plays in our area
supporting students who have been disengaged from mainstream schooling. And finally a
quick thank you to Colin Brooks MP and Bronwyn Halfpenny MP, our colleagues who
have been working with us on this issue, particularly Bronwyn who's electorate covers
the Epping campus of Pavilion and who I know has been talking to a lot of staff, students
and families. If you have any questions at all about this issue just get in touch with
our office or Colin's or Bronwyn's.

on Saturday evenings when the current wait is 30 minutes that will come down to every 20 minutes
and then on Sunday mornings before 10am when there is the current quite long wait of 40 minutes
that will also come down to every 20 minutes. Now obviously these are not the busiest times on
the network but a lot of people have raised them with us and I think that's because they're
times when many of us are making a one-off decision about whether we take the train or
take the car for a trip into the city and I think we all know that those long wait times
especially if you're unlucky enough to miss the train can be pretty stressful. They can throw
your plans out and they can leave you thinking it'll just be easier to take the car next time

been announced as part of the upcoming state budget so that is for the next financial year
which starts on the 1st of July but as soon as we have more details about the timetable
changes we'll let you know.

PRESTON MARKET UPDATE — there has been renewed discussion about development at Preston Market, following the sale of the Tarascio family’s component to their joint venture partners, the Medich family, in August last year.

Any such development would take years to plan — and years to build, across multiple stages.

However, if anyone is interested, there is a large amount of information online about what state government planning provisions would apply. Some of the key requirements are:

— ensure the market buildings with heritage significance are substantially retained, including the large murals, and maintain a working market with a minimum floor area of 12,700 m^2 

— provide approx 1,200 dwellings, including social and affordable housing, with a discretionary maximum of 14 storeys at the northern end and 4 storeys at the southern end 

— include approx 27,500 m^2 of retail floor space, and 5,000 m^2 of office floor space 

— provide a public open space adjacent to the market with a minimum area of 2,700 m^2 and a public open space adjacent to Preston Station of approx 1,000 m^2, with the ownership of both to be transferred to Darebin Council 

— encourage a modal shift to active and public transport 

— ensure adequate car parking for the market and other uses

— encourage loading, servicing and car parking areas to be located underground 

— encourage best-practice environmentally sustainable development outcomes in line with statewide commitments to net zero emissions, and achieve an average 0.5 stars above the prevailing NatHERS requirement for each building 

— provide electric charging points for bicycles and cars 

— provide for the use of alternatives to gas 

— deliver appropriate development staging to allow continuity of market trade throughout the redevelopment of the precinct and to support the viability of business for stall holders.

Note that if any development did proceed, it would probably begin on the two sites west of the train line at St Georges/Murray and St Georges/Cramer. They have maximum heights of 13 and 8 storeys respectively.
transcript:
Hi, there's been some renewed discussion about development at Preston Market, so I thought
I'd just recap where things were up to. As most people probably know, there are multiple
landlords across the Preston Market site, but the majority of the properties were
purchased by the Medich family back in 2004 in a joint venture with the Tarasco family.
And pretty much for the last 20 years, that joint venture has continuously sought
planning permission for two controversial propositions. The first was to move most
of the traders out of the existing buildings and into a new double-storey building built
here on the Aldi car park site so that it would have faced Cramer Street. Once it was
completed, the existing buildings on the western side were going to be demolished.
Suffice to say that was not popular with most people in the community. It was temporarily
blocked by Darebin Council on a number of occasions. And then it was permanently
blocked by our state government in 2023 when we put robust, proper heritage
protections on the existing buildings, ensuring that they had to be kept and taking that
particular option off the table. But the second controversial proposal was to build
apartments over the car parks, especially here on the western side, close to Preston
train station. If we're honest, that was also not popular with a lot of people in
the community. But in contrast, it was mostly supported by Darebin
councillors of all political persuasions, green Labor and independents.
And in fact, at one point, the majority owners actually had approved building
permits for a 14-storey building up on Murray Road, which I understand was going
to have a Coles under it. But in essence, every political party, every independent,
every community group, including the Save the Preston Market group, all said that they
were OK with at least 800 apartments and a story height of at least 10 stories in
places. And that is because it's good public policy. Building more homes close
to public transport is a big, important urban project for Melbourne.
It's good for congestion. It's good for emissions. It's good for housing
affordability. Obviously, the key question here, the specific question is
whether it is also, in this case, good for the Preston Market and good for
the local area. And probably that really depends a lot on the more detailed
open space, canopy cover, infrastructure contributions, pedestrian access,
bike access, all those things that we will debate if and when we see a proposal.
Finally, there is a good discussion about public acquisition. Darebin
councillor doing a feasibility study into that at the moment. Again,
it sort of depends on the apartment question. Public acquisition for the
purpose of building apartments on the site is obviously a very different
proposition to public acquisition for the purpose of blocking apartments
on the site. We will see what the Darebin council study has to say about
those two possibilities. We do expect at some point for the majority
owners to put forward a proposal. There is a rumour it might be
sometime soon. We guess it might look something like the Darebin
council vision from 2022, at least in terms of its scale.
But whatever it looks like, there will then be a long period of
planning consideration, planning permits, building permits for every
stage that will spend many years, that will probably spend many
elections. Nothing will happen particularly quickly and there will be
a lot of opportunity for public debate, including amongst people who
shop here all the time and love it, including amongst the traders of
course who are the heart of the market. All of those people have the
opportunity to put their views forward and the Minister in Savarishy
makes any decisions will take all of that into account.

COST OF LIVING RELIEF — a reminder that applications for the Victorian Labor Government’s 20% rego rebate will open on Monday 1 June through the Service Victoria app and website, and close on Friday 31 July.
 
Along with free public transport and half-price fares for the rest of the year, this rebate is helping Victorians manage the cost-of-living impacts associated with the conflict in the Middle East.
 
The rebate applies to eligible vehicles registered in an individual’s name. It is not available for vehicles registered to companies.
transcript:
Just a quick reminder about the 20% rego rebate. As most people know, the state government has
responded to the cost of living pressures that have arisen due to the conflict in the Middle
East through two major measures. The first is making public transport free, as it will be for
the rest of this month, and then half price for the remainder of the year. And the second
is providing a one-off 20% vehicle registration rebate. Now this rebate will apply to light
vehicles registration payments that have been made in this financial year. So that is between
the 1st of July 2025 to the 30th of June 2026. So for most people, it will be a rebate on a
registration that you've already paid. If you've already paid, just to be clear, you've not
missed out, this is for you. Now it is available, however, only to individuals,
not to companies, and it is capped at two rebates per person. Applications will open
on Monday 1st of June through the Service Victoria app and website and close on Friday
31st of July. We'll put out a reminder once those applications open and some more details.

My question is for the Minister for Water and my question is, what is the Victorian
Government's policy position on putting bike paths and vegetation on land that has water
pipes underneath it?
I ask this question because we announced last year that we were going to plant an
additional 1,000 trees across Preston and Reservoir, including along parts of the
Northern Pipe Trail, and we remain very committed to that project, but we have
run into the chAllange that there are some authorities and some decision makers
who seem to think you can't plant trees or put bike paths anywhere near any underground
asset.
Of course, we appreciate that it is important to protect those assets and of course there
are real maintenance costs involved, but at the same time we note that there are bike
paths and trees on top of underground assets right across this city, including elsewhere
on the Northern Pipe Trail, and we believe that the ESE and other authorities should
treat this as a normal cost of doing business and not use it as an excuse or
a reason to stop urban greening projects or stop active transport projects.
Any advice or information that the Minister can provide to us on this matter would
be greatly appreciated.

ERIC STREET UPDATE — the two public housing walk-ups at 15–17 Eric Street have been proposed for demolition.

In the reel, I say that the Minister for Planning has given permission for demolition to proceed. To be completely accurate, a final decision hasn’t been made yet. Homes Victoria has completed the consultation and is preparing a planning application for demolition. If you have any questions or concerns, we can still follow up.

Some other points of note from reading the reports…

— The planning report says the vacant apartments are no longer suitable for housing due to their age, poor condition, fire damage, poor environmental performance and the difficulty of bringing them up to current building standards.

— The heritage report says the statement of significance in the original heritage overlay was not accurate in describing the blocks as “an unusual development of pre-cast concrete walk-up flats”. Nonetheless, it recommends the preparation of an archival-quality photographic record in accordance with Heritage Victoria’s guidelines.

— The preliminary arboricultural report assesses 24 trees within the site itself. It says the concept design may allow some trees in the central courtyard to be retained, including two mature melaleucas. Most trees on the site are exotics.
transcript:
Local residents be aware of the good news that the Eric Street estate buildings, which
were in awful condition and where there were significant safety concerns, are now going
to be demolished. Now there was a long standing chAllange here that we've mentioned previously
which was that Council had an old heritage overlay on the buildings that prevented
any demolition or redevelopment, but fortunately the State Government Minister for Planning
Sonia Kilkenny, we're very grateful that she has stepped in and used some new powers
that she has to give permission for this demolition to occur. Now that wasn't a
decision that was made lightly and there is a very detailed report about it that
we can send to anyone who's interested. It also doesn't mean that a final decision
has been made about the future of the site, but given that the specific powers that
the Minister used relate to social housing projects, we do think it is most likely
that we will see a new social housing project here on Eric Street at some point in the
future and that will continue the strong growth of social housing across Preston
and Reservoir that we've seen in recent years, including of course the site up
at Keon Park on Johnson Street that we posted about earlier today. As always, if
you have any questions about any of these projects, just let us know.

The Reservoir Police Station counter service will close permanently from 6:00 pm this evening.

Those who attended the Darebin Neighbourhood Policing Forum earlier this month would have heard Victoria Police explain the rationale for the change. The aim is to ensure officers spend as much time as possible patrolling and responding to serious incidents.

For emergencies or urgent police attendance, call 000.

For non-urgent police assistance, call 131 444.

Police reports can be made online through the Victoria Police website, at Preston Police Station between 9:00 am and 9:00 pm every day, or at Fawkner Police Station 24/7.
transcript:
Just letting everyone know that the Reservoir Police Station counter service will close today permanently
and that the Preston Police Station counter service will now operate from 9am to 9pm seven days a week.
Now it's important to be clear that this does not at all mean that the Reservoir Police Station is closing.
In fact, there will still be exactly the same number of police officers here 24-7 as there have always been
and in fact it means that there will be more police available for the most important things they do
which is patrolling in the Reservoir community and responding to critical incidents when people need them.
They can't do that if they're stuck behind a desk.
Now, my brother used to work at the old Reservoir Police Station a long time ago
and I know that back then they would only have two officers patrolling all of Reservoir overnight
and then he or someone else would often be stuck behind the old front desk for the entire night
realistically not doing a great deal with their time.
Now we have a much bigger, better police station.
We have a dedicated family violence unit here and without going to the operational details
we certainly have more police doing more patrols more often and these changes will just further help that.
Of course, if you do need police for any serious reason just call 000.

video_description: KEON PARK UPDATE — we’ve nearly finished doorknocking all the houses between Johnson Street and Cheddar Road. We will take the feedback regarding the Johnson Street development into meetings within government next week.
transcript:
Hi, we've just been doing on Keon Park talking to people mainly about the new social housing
development that's going to go in right here. We have now managed to talk to nearly every house
between Johnson Street and Cheddar Road. Once we have finished that, we will compile all that
feedback together for some meetings within government that have been organized around
this issue next week. But I just want to note one thing that I personally think is a little
bit disappointing and that is we are now only 140 days from the Victorian state election.
People are certainly now beginning to talk about how they're going to vote and yet no other
party or candidate appears to want to engage in reservoir on local reservoir issues. Not on
this issue. We see nothing on the changes to the police station that were announced recently,
nothing on the changes to the restrictive covenant that are very important to a lot of
people on the Maryland side. I think if we're completely fair, Serena, who's a
Victorian socialist candidate, did do a thing about reservoir enabled house the other week
and Rachel from Animal Justice is actually well known for her local advocacy, especially
around Edwardes Lake. But the Greens and the Liberals, who traditionally are those parties with
the higher vote, have been completely absent. And you might have seen that Jess Wilson,
the leader of the Liberal Party, has been making a big song and dance about the fact
that apparently this month she is going to try and visit every part of Victoria to talk to
local people about the local issues that matter to them. But certainly whatever that
grand tour is, it has not yet involved reservoir, even though reservoir is the
sixth biggest suburb in Melbourne. We've seen no sign of Liberals at all. And as
we understand it, they can't even find a candidate here. They couldn't find a
candidate in council elections. And all of that is really disappointing because I think
at this point in time, in particular, we know there is quite a bit of alienation out there.
We know that there are some people who are thinking about voting one nation for the
first time, in part because they feel disconnected from the system. And that is really concerning.
But surely the best thing we can do about it, no matter what our party is,
is to go and knock on people's doors, knock on those people's doors, talk to them
about actual concrete, real local community issues, things where they have some lived
experience and where you can take the discussion and the debate away from the
internet bubbles and away from the Facebook groups and have that proper person to person
interaction, talk to them what their neighbours might think, but most importantly, remind
people that their views, their personal views, really do matter because of course they do.
Anyway, that's what we're doing here in Keyon Park. We'll keep doing it. We'll do it
elsewhere in Reservoir and Preston, of course. Hopefully other candidates will join us shortly.

video_description:
No club is responsible for the actions of every supporter. But every club is responsible for the culture it fosters and the standards it enforces.

Incident details at @[719673342:2048:Sherele Moody], Football Victoria and Preston Lions Football Club
transcript:
Some of you might have seen that on Saturday a group of Preston Lions supporters put up
some very racist and misogynist banners that were directed towards Greek Victorians and
Greek Victorian women in particular. Those banners were taken down quickly by the security
at the ground but photos of them then circulated on Instagram and other social media platforms
apparently through some of these so-called ultras accounts. We understand that as of
today the people involved in this behaviour have been identified and we are expecting
the club to put out a statement shortly setting out the very serious consequences
that they will face and then Football Victoria will announce further disciplinary action
we expect at some point next week. And of course as a state government we introduced
new laws last year, strong laws that made it easier to prosecute racial or gender
based vilification including in serious cases as a criminal offence and including in very
serious cases with potential jail terms. But I think it's also important with this
particular incident to mention the additional context anyone who grew up playing soccer
in the 80s or 90s will know that certain intra-European rivalries have been part of
the game in this state for a very long time and I think sometimes we can make the mistake
of romanticising that sort of stuff, I think I've been guilty of that, seeing
it as some sort of authentic working class multiculturalism. It's not that and surely
this incident reminds us how much it's not that. The clubs might be that but
the conflict is not. It has always been ugly, it has often been explicitly racist,
it has often been very personal and unfortunately and as was the case on Saturday it's
often involved kids. I remember seeing Serbian and Croatian under 12s or under 14s
maybe saying awful things to each other because they were being egged on by older
members of their clubs and so I think it's important to recognise that we have had
behaviour occur here that has caused people to feel objectified, it has caused them
to feel racially vilified, none of that is acceptable but it has also separately
and additionally caused them to feel unsafe because people are deliberately escalating
this perceived nationalist conflict and that is something that nobody wants. So hopefully
the club and particularly Football Victoria will address that as well through their
statements and through their actions. As a state government we'll continue our work
to tackle vilification and racial hatred and gender based hatred but also our important
reforms to unmask anonymous accounts on the internet which have played a role here
as well and hopefully between all those things we can finally get to the point
where we can talk about soccer, enjoy soccer, enjoy last minute upset wins and all the
great things about the game without also having to talk about this abhorrent behaviour
that has been part of the game locally in Victoria for way too long.

video_description:
MERRILANDS COVENANT UPDATE — we have asked the Minister for Planning to make all applications to remove or vary restrictive covenants Type 3 applications.

This would preserve notice, objection and VCAT review rights.
transcript:
My adjournment matter concerns the controversial local issue of the Merrilands single dwelling
covenant. I actually addressed this issue earlier this week, Speaker, but I would like
to take the opportunity this evening to make a formal adjournment action request of the
Minister for Planning. I will come to the exact details of that action request shortly.
By way of background, the Merrilands covenant is a private legal agreement that has been
in place since that area was subdivided, mostly following World War II. In essence,
it prevents most landowners north of Broadhurst in that part of the reservoir from subdividing
their property into townhouses or apartments. I should say, Speaker, it is a very popular
policy in that part of the world. Many people moved there specifically because
of the existence of the covenant and, of course, made a very large financial decision,
a very big life decision, to move into that part of the world.
But clearly, also, Speaker, it is an arrangement that is at odds with our government's
housing policy. We are not seeking to stop townhouses or apartments and, in fact, on
the contrary, we are seeking to build more townhouses and more apartments particularly
close to transport hubs and particularly close to train stations in order to reduce
emissions, to deal with congestion, to improve housing affordability, but most importantly
to give people, and particularly young people, the opportunity to live close to jobs, to
education and the cultural or social opportunities that they would like.
So that is an important policy to us and so we have reformed the Planning and Environment
Act to make it easier to remove the restrictive covenant.
However, there does remain, Speaker, a critical question in this particular policy
area, and that is whether those applications to remove the covenant will be Type 2 or
Type 3 applications. I would just like to put on the record my very strong support
for the idea that they should be Type 3 applications and, in fact, my adjournment
action for the Minister for Planning is to make any application to remove or vary
the covenant a Type 3 application. And I think, Speaker, that that is consistent
with the way we have approached our planning reforms generally. Of course, we are encouraging
making it easier, encouraging people to build homes, making it easier to build homes right
across Victoria, but of course we are doing so in a way that reflects the existing
planning structure that has been built up over a long time and has set planning
expectations over a long time, and I think it makes sense that in doing so we acknowledge
that restrictive covenants, whilst an unusual part of the system, are nonetheless a legitimate
part of the system and should be treated that way. And I note in closing, Speaker,
that we have a clear position on this, but the Greens can date, the Liberal can
date, do not.

I do want to take this opportunity, Acting Speaker, to acknowledge the role of the Member
for Bendigo East, the very long-standing role of the Member for Bendigo East in that leadership
team. We have been hugely grateful locally for the former Premier's help with us on a number
of significant local issues, but also just on a personal note, Acting Speaker, I know that

But we've also spent too much time, Acting Speaker, in the Royal Children's Hospital.
No one wants to spend time there, but we will actually be back there on Friday for

And I just want to express our gratitude to the former Premier for her understanding and

But as I say, all of the remarkable staff at the Royal Children's Hospital who,

our family as well.

acting Speaker by the fact that the member for Niddrie and the Minister in his then role

that we got good outcomes for local Preston residents in this case and we look forward to

Hi, we're back in Keon Park and I just wanted to summarise where things are at with the
61 Johnson Street social housing development. The first important point to make of course
is that as a Labor Government we absolutely support social housing. And we support the
specific model that is being used here, where our colleagues in the Federal Labor
Government are providing the funding, the subsidy to make this important project happen.
We are not going to do that thing that sometimes other political parties and other
politicians do, including sometimes the Greens, where they say they support new
social housing in theory. Everyone always says they support it in theory and then
people find an excuse to oppose specific projects when they happen in the real world.
We're not doing that, we support this specific project and we're certainly not
going to say no to a Federal Government subsidy of over $20,000 per apartment
per year that will make a real difference for local people in need.
However, a second important thing also to say is that we absolutely believe and
agree that any form of Government supported housing must of course be safe
for residents and safe for other community members. Now 99% of the time it is.
There are roughly 4,000 people who live in public housing or community
housing across Preston and Reservoir and as we all know, the vast, vast majority
of those people are fantastic, wonderful people who make a really positive
contribution to the economy, to the community I should say, and the economy
as well. But at any given point in time, in our experience, there will be
a handful, maybe 10 or 20 across all the different locations, half a percent
maybe, who are causing some issues, sometimes serious issues for other
residents and neighbours. It does happen, it happens in private housing
as well of course, but wherever it happens, you do need landlords, in this
case social housing teams who are prepared to act quickly to provide
people with the support they need and sometimes to make the tough decisions
to issue compliance orders or even transfer people out of a specific
building with the appropriate supports. And again, this is a point of
difference between the political parties, but it is something we believe
in very strongly. It is possible, absolutely possible to have perfectly
safe community housing as most community housing is, as long as you
are a bit proactive about just ensuring that people are matched with
the level of support that they need and a consequence of that, an unavoidable
consequence of that triaged or streamed arrangement, is that the
very, very small percentage of people who behave in a repeatedly
antisocial manner or even in an outright illegal manner, will have
and should have a smaller set of options available to them, which
will not include developments like this one, like this particular
development, that if you look at their funding model, this one is
funded at the low support need end of the spectrum. Now we've made
that point to Ministers on a number of occasions and will continue
to do so. And then finally, the other major issue people have is
parking. Derriban Council are currently undertaking a review of
parking in the Johnson Street area, but unfortunately, it will not
be ready in time to provide input into this project. We have
said to the relevant Ministers, we don't think that Keyon Park
is a walkable neighbourhood in the way that the project claims it
is. We think people probably will have and need cars, and so
the project will need more parking, just like the Trinity
and Capella apartments next door. People have raised a lot of
other issues as well. We will provide more details of that in
the comments as well as details on the next steps, but we just
want to cover off on those three key issues of parking,
safety and our overall support for this important social
housing project right here in Keyon Park.

Labor believes in a coordinated approach to crime prevention and law enforcement.

That means investing in police, PSOs and the services that address the underlying causes of violence.
transcript:
We recently announced that there will be more PSO patrols here at Northland and that they will now continue until the end of 2027.
And I just want to flag that this general question, this question about whether we think that more local law enforcement resources are a good thing
is really shaping up as a key point of difference in the upcoming election here in Preston and Reservoir.
Obviously as a Labor government, as Labor representatives, we support more police, more PSOs and more law enforcement generally.
But on the other hand, the Greens, who realistically are the other party that I think could win here, who could become local representatives,
they broadly speaking have the reverse view. They oppose more police, they oppose more PSOs and they oppose more law enforcement powers.
And we saw that particular difference in views play out in Parliament last week.
We had a bill, an important bill, that introduced some new things called workplace protection orders.
And these orders allow the courts to ban violent or threatening customers from the workplace.
And they've been called for in fact by workers right here at Northland and they've been called for particularly strongly by the SDA,
which is the Retail Workers Union. We as a Labor government voted for them, the Greens voted against them because of this difference in views.
Now I want to be clear about what that difference is. It is not a difference on all matters in the justice portfolio.
In fact there is a bill coming next week on family violence that I'm sure Labor and the Greens will agree on.

VISY UPDATE – if you are concerned about the odours from the Visy recycling plant, please sign the parliamentary petition via the link in the comments. 

BACKGROUND INFO

Visy has been producing cardboard packaging at the Radford Road site since 1959. The recycling plant opened in 1983.

There is some debate about when the odour issue started. Many people date it to roughly 2020, when Visy began recycling more water and using more household feedstock (which includes more food residue than industrial feedstock).

Bacteria in the plant’s recycled water systems produced sulphides and volatile fatty acids, which can cause strong odours.

Following complaints from residents, the Environment Protection Authority (EPA) issued a series of notices to Visy requiring the company to investigate and rectify the issue. The rectification measures included:

— introducing a bacteria control program (from 2020)
— increasing the use of fresh water for flushing (from 2021)
— switching back to industrial feedstock (from 2022)
— sealing roof vents and building gaps (2022–2025)
— extending exhaust systems and installing new stacks and fans (2021–2026).

Visy claims that the changes have resulted in a 91% reduction in measured odour units at the plant.

However, we don’t believe the reduction experienced in the community has been anywhere near that amount.

We have doorknocked all homes within 500 metres of the plant: once in 2022 and again this year.

While different people have different senses of smell, the odours remain a serious problem for many households. In 2022, we estimated that more than 200 households felt the odours were having a major negative impact on their lives. In 2026, we estimate that more than 100 households continue to be affected that way.

A local resident, Frieda De Doncker, has started a petition asking the EPA to impose further, urgent odour control requirements. We support that ask.

We are sponsoring the petition to provide further evidence about the number of households affected.

We will continue to raise the issue in parliament and with the minister.

Concerns about artificial intelligence and data centres have been raised locally.

It seems likely that the key regulation will be determined at the national level. National Cabinet is meeting about the issue today. However, we have raised residents’ concerns with the relevant state ministers.

There are no plans for large-scale compute centres in Preston or Reservoir.
transcript:
Deputy Speaker, I normally raise fairly specific Preston Reservoir matters, but we did have
a debate earlier this week about data centres and AI, and I wanted to pick up some of the
points from that debate. I won't repeat the important points that were made about planning,
energy use and water use, but rather I'd like to pick up on this important notion
that data centres are not really data centres. As we spoke about, these are centres that
are not full of traditional file servers, they are not storing people's data or photos
or anything else. Rather, they are predominantly filled with processing units, GPUs, and what
they actually are are the giant artificial brains that we are building to do our thinking
for us when we use applications like Clawd and ChatGPT. They should properly, Deputy
Speaker, be called compute centres or inference centres, and I do think, I don't think
it's deliberate, but I think calling them data centres makes it sound more innocuous
and underplays just how radical this technology is.
A second thing, Deputy Speaker, that I think causes people to underestimate how radical
this technology is, is the fact that the standard models of Clawd or ChatGPT that
we have on our phones, whilst remarkable technology, are very neutered compared to
the extraordinary capacity of the frontier models that these companies have built already,
let alone the ones they are attempting to build. We have this strange situation
with AI, the reverse of what normally happens. What normally happens is that the people,
the public outside an industry are worried, the people inside an industry, be it fracking
or the nuclear industry, are normally less worried. That's the normal course of things.
With AI, it is the other way round. Even the criticisms of the Greens and the
Victorian socialists are mainly focusing on things on water and energy use. They
are important issues, but when you listen to some of the software engineers and researchers
who have built these frontier models and used them day to day, they are seriously
worried about what it will look like when we deploy at massive scale these artificial
creatures that can outthink humans across a broad domain of tasks. They are worried
not only what that will do economically, but what it might do in a military sense
and what it might do in a very fundamental, existential way for humanity. Of course,
there are all sorts of positive things that can come from this, and I want to be clear
that I am just talking about the long tail risks, but as someone with a little bit of
work experience in this sector, the thing that I am most worried now for my children
is no longer climate change, it's not nuclear weapons, it is where AI might go. I just
encourage the other parties, the Greens and the Liberals, who I think have not
fully yet engaged with this issue, to think clearly about it as the Minister and as our
Labor Government are doing so, because I do think, Deputy Speaker, that this will be
one of the most significant regulatory chAllanges that we in the Victorian
Government and indeed governments across the globe face in the coming decades.

We made a submission supporting stronger controls on non-therapeutic nitrous oxide sales.
transcript:
Thank you, Deputy Speaker. My adjournment matter is for the Minister for Casino, Gaming
and Liquor Regulation. The action I seek is for the Minister to prohibit registered
tobacco retailers from selling nitrous oxide products, known as NANGs. Members in this
place will be aware that nitrous oxide is a medical analgesic, a legitimate one,
but it is used recreationally and it is used recreationally a lot in Preston and
Reservoir. The public health evidence shows that there are significant risks attached
with that use. To be clear, it is not by any means the most dangerous recreational drug,
but the coroner reported in 2025 on the tragic death of a 26-year-old man identified in the
coroner's report as RBJ, who died in Elston Wick in 2023 from nitrous oxide suffocation.
I might just quote from the coroner's report that RBJ is remembered as a beautiful,
caring and loving young man. RBJ loved computers and was great at building and
programming them. As someone who shares those or certainly shared those enthusiasms,
I think of RBJ and the tragic case of his death and the effect it, of course, would have had on
his family and loved ones. I note the coroner's reporting of the risks of nitrous
oxide in that case and the identification of 11 other cases this century where nitrous oxide
has been associated with someone's passing. Eight of them have occurred, Deputy Speaker,
in the last five years. I note, in addition, the coroner's recommendation that our government
look into stronger regulations of nitrous oxide, such as those found in South Australia
or those that are due to commence in New South Wales as a result of some changes
introduced by the Minns government in November of this year. For a long time, Deputy Speaker,
the chAllange with regulating the retail sales of nitrous oxide is that, of course,
there are legitimate uses of it associated with food preparation, but we all know,
Deputy Speaker, that the common model that we see is that it's sold in convenience stores
alongside tobacco, legal tobacco, sometimes illegal tobacco, confectionery, energy drinks,
sometimes vapes. We all know that model, Deputy Speaker, and I think we do have an
opportunity to disrupt that particular model and at least curtail some of the sales of
nangs in those convenience stores through our important tobacco licensing reforms. We now have
an enforcement regime. We have an inspection regime. We're building that out and we thus
have the opportunity to make it a condition of holding those tobacco licenses that people
don't sell nitrous oxide products. We'll do that primarily, I think, Deputy Speaker,
because of the important health reasons that I've set out and the tragic case that I touched
upon, but also for environmental and amenity reasons. The nitrous oxide canisters are hard
to dispose of as well, but as I say, primarily for health reasons, I put forward this particular
suggestion to the Minister and I thank him and his department for their consideration.

ever taken any form of gifts or corporate hospitality from a property developer. I
don't own shares in any of their companies. I don't own shares directly in any companies
at all, except through my superannuation. I don't own any investment properties, so
I don't have that potential alignment of interest. I've in fact only ever owned
one property full stop, and that is our current family home in Preston. And as
it turns out, I should say on this particular project, the developers who
involved Hallmark have unfortunately refused to respond to our calls and
emails about the project. So not only can we say, you know, we don't
generally hang out with these people, but in this case, we have literally not
spoken a single word to the developers. And as I say, I think that's actually
unfortunate because we did have some things to raise with them. But integrity
in politics is important. If you do at any stage have any concerns about any
Victorian politician, you can and should raise them with IBAC, the
Independent Board-Based Anti-Corruption Commission. We actually increased their
powers earlier this year to investigate exactly these sort of
issues. You can also raise any concerns with Victoria Police, with
the Victorian Ombudsman or with the new Parliamentary Workplace Standards
and Integrity Commission, which is another fully independent, well
resourced body that our government established in 2024. It is important
always to be vigilant about integrity in politics. And so should you need
them, we will put contact details for those organisations in the comments.

transcript:
Hi everyone, we're here in Keon Park where we've got an update on the 61 Johnson Street
project that we're providing to people. I'll just run through it quickly.
With respect to the tenancies in the cohort, the site will be predominantly for over 55s
and is intended for tenants with low support needs. The community housing provider,
National Affordable Housing Victoria, will interview prospective tenants to determine
suitability for a lower support environment and also whether they own a vehicle.
And that brings us to parking. Unfortunately, we've not had a win there. In fact,
there will be 57 resident car park places, which is less than the 60 we had before.
It is still more than the 48 required under the planning scheme and more than the amount
that Darebin Council advocated for. But we have been advised by Homes Victoria that the
intended over 55s cohort tend to have less vehicles per household, approximately 0.4 per
household, and that vehicle ownership will be considered during tenancy interviews.
And then people have raised the issue of fresh food and the availability of fresh
groceries in the Johnson Street area. We have not had a win with that. There will be retail on
the ground floor, but we're still working on trying to confirm what sort of retail that will
be. With respect to the housing mix, the proposed one and two bedroom apartments remain.
We understand or are told that they reflect demand on the Victorian housing register,
particularly amongst this over 55s cohort. And then with respect to community safety
and management of the block, we've been told that the apartments have been repositioned
somewhat so that they better overlook the station plaza and the pedestrian
walkway that's behind me here. It will have improved lighting and sight lines.
The management office has been relocated to the ground floor and the community housing
provider will have people there Monday to Friday, nine to five, in normal business
hours if people have things that they want to raise. We have requested a copy of the
consultation report, though unfortunately we still haven't been able to obtain that.
But if you have any questions about this update, please just let us know.
